Batavia. To the Honorable Lord Joan Maatzuijcker, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords of the Council of India. Amboina. A missive from the Honorable Governor and the Council there, addressed to Your Honors, dated the 5th of May 1668.

Your Honors, Most Esteemed, Highly Respected, Valiant and Wise Gentlemen, and Generous Lords, High Commanding Gentlemen,

In this current year, God be praised, with the safe passage of the fleet ships Pegu and Witte Leeuw, as well as the Yacht Meliskerken, all via Makassar, have arrived safely with us. Your Honors' pleasant letters, with their attachments, dated the 11th of January and 23rd of February, together with the Cargoes for this province that were loaded therein, according to the respective invoices, for which liberal provision—especially now that the long delay of the fatherland's ships at the Cape and the shortage of provisions has caused much scarcity—we believe we have sufficient reason to thank Your Honors, which we do hereby, wishing that it had pleased God that in return a more ample supply had been able to come to Your Honors for the relief of the Company's heavy burdens, as unfortunately it has not, the harvest also coming so late that we have had to hold back the fleet ship Klaverskerken for somewhat longer than our desire would have been, in order to fulfill Your Honors' and the Esteemed Superintendent's orders, had we wished to send it away empty. But considering that Your Honors desire both the cloves and the fleet ship speedily, nothing else can be done but to perform all due diligence and to take patience further. The hooker-boat the Pimpelmees, sent by Your Honors to the fleet on the 9th of January, with letters and the loaded Cargo (as the chief officers say) was indeed in sight of the castles at Makassar, but nevertheless no word was heard there of our ships or flags, whereupon it proceeded via Buton and arrived here safely on the 19th of February. The thoughts at that time were that the Esteemed Superintendent with the force must have been at Bima, to conclude there the end of the glorious successes. However, the following boats and letters from His Excellency soon revealed to us that we had been mistaken, the ships having lain at anchor behind the island before the Company's Castle Rotterdam. Also, the scruple, given the lack of knowledge in Amboina on the 5th of May 1668 of the success, would not have made them bold enough to come closer and to see properly. Yet the delay does not appear to be great from his aforementioned letters, since he finds himself sufficiently provisioned with everything, and has moreover provided us with various provisions, ammunition, etc., per Vlieland and Klaverskerken, to the amount of ƒ 23,173:—:2:, these boats having been sent there on the 30th of January and early March, and arrived here on the 22nd of February and 14th of March respectively, in good condition.

Regarding the last shipment, according to Your Honors' orders, the fleet ship Witte Leeuw is being held back, which in the meantime is still serving God's work on the fortifications, and the Meliskerken will, as soon as it is loaded with 7 barrels of gunpowder and some timber, if the same can be loaded therein (given the lack of a cargo hatch), also depart shortly for Makassar, as well as the Vlieland, if we find that it is not capable of rendering any particular service due to its great leakiness, which would be worthy of the delay. But it is very apparent that the aforementioned hooker will have to remain for the last shipment, and perhaps even over the year, to serve as an advisor in all circumstances, since the misfortune, to our sorrow, has befallen us that the small Yacht Boero, anchored on the same island on the north side at the place Sieko Mourassa and lying in the loading of planks, was wrecked on the 19th of February last by an unexpected northerly wind. The Provincial Captain named Evert Caspersz. of Amsterdam was brought to trial over this, which trial is still continuing. Otherwise, nothing can be said regarding the life and conduct of the aforementioned person. Meanwhile, this loss has deprived us of much convenience. We therefore hope that if the aforementioned hooker, as stated, were deemed necessary to remain here, we would not be doing wrong thereby.

The aftermath of the cloves, which is to be expected toward August next, will, according to all appearances, also be quite small—at any rate, not so large that the Witte Leeuw would have sufficient space to take it in—from which it appears how meager and lean Your Honors and the Esteemed Masters will find the Losted [uncertain: possibly a type of cargo or vessel] spice from this year's fruits, which the Almighty will hopefully make good for the coming

to remain, so that we would not be doing wrong thereby. The aftermath of the cloves, which is to be expected toward August next, will, according to all appearances, also be quite small—at any rate, not so large that the Witte Leeuw would have sufficient space to take it in—from which it appears how meager and lean Your Honors and the Esteemed Masters will find the Losted spice from this year's fruits, which the Almighty will hopefully make good for the coming year, as is to be hoped, and which is also trusted. To this end, a multitude of young trees are to be planted for the first time. At the visitation for the observation of the previously ordered plantation, as much as possible the hand is being held, according to our instruction set thereon, to be seen by resolution of the 30th of January, not doubting that the feared negligence will thereby be prevented. Amboina, the 5th of May 1668. This extraordinary visitation will take a long and tedious time before it is completed everywhere, since the visitors must examine all the trees, both small and large, and judge and report on their condition, with the taking of an oath that everything has been found as it should be. To this end are qualified the Ensign Jacques Compagon together with a sergeant with their assistants, and Your Honors will see the effect thereof in due time. Meanwhile, we note that some have been more concerned with maintaining their assigned number in the third [uncertain: possibly a measurement or administrative division], than with attending to the success, since many are set so close together that they deprive each other of nourishment. And for this reason it will be necessary with particular care to order the required distance noted in the aforementioned instruction. But here lies yet another matter that is tied up, which seems to have caused concern, for the successive orders also bring with them that each household must maintain 80 plants. Meanwhile, some throw away [uncertain: possibly "abandon" or "neglect"] for the lack of land to find the necessary space. If, however, this proposal should have the desired effect, as it should, and as is confirmed by the visitors, then it will be necessary to deviate from the order as much as is proper. This perhaps will cause no small offense to others where the matter does not lie thus, since what is new is often heard—the sluggishness of the Islanders toward clove cultivation, claiming that scarcely anyone finds themselves capable, with their own people, of harvesting their cloves with a good crop, but must invite their friends and hire other households to do so, at such great cost of entertainment, etc., that the owner in the end has little left over, and gives them little encouragement for that work. To this we give more credence, the merchant Sir Kumphius of Hitoe having noted on the 16th of February last regarding this matter how the Jutsje Faij, at the insistence of the visitor, namely that many shoots in one place, not standing in good soil, should be transferred to another, and thus the cultivation be promoted, gave as an answer, among other things, whether he was a god, that he could make the trees grow according to our wishes. Furthermore, having seen how Your Excellency from the resolution of the Esteemed Superintendent taken with the council has become clear, that for weighty reasons it seemed advisable to persevere on the land of Houamosel, otherwise Warnoele, with the uprooting of the clove trees there, and that Manipa is also entirely bereft of them, yet the Esteemed Company against the many meager [harvests of] Amboina on the 5th of May 1668, has grown a place of recourse. needs, which Your Excellency kindly desired to see designated, so it is that we after preceding deliberation declared ourselves thereupon, to know of no other place to point out than that very same which by resolution aforementioned was rejected, namely on Houamosel, where the fertility is so great that some experienced men wish to maintain an impossibility of complete uprooting of the clove trees, or new quantities of shoots will be found again each time, it appearing that land by nature above all others is endowed in abundance with this costly spice. If Your Excellency then deems the matter thus important, that from the necessity a virtue should be made, we shall take the liberty to conduct ourselves regarding this according to a discourse held in a certain letter to the Esteemed Governor Jacob Cops sent to Banda, dated the 21st of October 1667, which for the sake of convenience goes herewith, serving only for correction thereof, considering on this side of Loehoe

Meanwhile, we may not pass over in silence how here frequently it has been found that the trees by a certain kind of small worm are so bored that the natural sap and root flowing out thereof causes the tree to die in a short time, which we would lightly, under the common accidents of plants, let pass without concern, if we were not informed from many sides that this pestilential and creeping worm now more than ever heard of rages in the clove trees, whereby diverse, both young, middling, as well as old fruit-bearing trees come to perish. We will pray to God that it be no rod of His punishing hand, but that our further advice shall bring forth a more pleasant matter, to which the new planting promises good occasion, as has been prepared here before. In fulfillment of the aforementioned Esteemed Superintendent's order, it has been attempted with all vigilance to uproot the trees on the places marked by the resolution, namely on Houamohel

By transport through the commissioned [official] to Erang felled according to report of the 25th of November inserted by the arriving letters, besides an innumerable quantity of young shoots: 89: 3300. The island Quelang by the aforementioned visitor: 327: 507. Boero by the ensign Jan Leipziq obtained, having been brought and uprooted by those of Omblou out of malice: 2702: 5449. Amblau by the Boeronese (the aforementioned ensign present) felled and spoiled: 292: 24. Totaling together clove trees: 4410 and 9280 nutmeg trees—which are certainly without doubt on Boero, and perhaps also on Amblau more will yet be discovered, to which the ensign Jan Leipziq does not fail in his duty. On Kelin about 8 or 9 miles inland from the bay Fanoene on Ceram (according to report made to us by the orangkaij [local chief] of Piroe) there would be held hidden by a certain orangkaij named Tikkesane about a hundred clove trees, of which half bear fruit, but the matter is not yet entirely certain, nor advisable without the Correcore's might, with caution, to inquire thereupon, which shall happen when the time has come thereto. Amkorinc I M. Bar. Amboina on the 5th of May 1668. Concerning the outcome of affairs at Makassar, our aforementioned Esteemed Lord Cornelis Speelman, Superintendent Admiral, War Commander, etc., has sent us word speedily by missive dated the 5th of December by the Chialoup Timor, which arrived here on the 22nd of the same month. Over which lordly victory, just as we have steadily prayed to the great God thereto, so His Majesty has been brought the solemn thanksgiving with joy over this great salvation, whereby the state of the Esteemed Company under Your Excellency's wise governance, through the means of the untiring diligence of the aforementioned lord, remains blessed. Therefore we then take the liberty to wish Your Excellency with this Conquest much luck and the Most High's

Therefore we then take the liberty to wish Your Excellency with this Conquest much luck and the Most High's further salutary governance. Regarding the war discipline therein, the order set by His aforementioned Esteemed [person] is observed, the plundering also remains forbidden under high penalty, and the Captain's duty shall further be to ensure good observance of both the one and the other. Concerning the militia, taking regard to the hand weapons of the soldiers, which were somewhat poorly maintained, we have on all the outlying places exchanged [them] for new and good ones. There remains yet for the proper defense of the Redoubts, where there are no fresh rivers or wells at hand, to procure some water tanks, since the wooden work of the Esteemed Company, costly as it falls, is immediately eaten through by the worm. His Esteemed [person] had well ordered to make some wooden water barrels, but the same could not be completed through lack of good jati [teak] planks. The redoubt Velsen on Hatuana to Homimoa, where one always had to fetch water about half an hour away, is after much seeking and digging from that deficiency relieved by the fortunate discovery of a water vein about 120 paces from the aforementioned redoubt, laying where now a very good well has been made. The redoubt Delff on Porto has also the aforementioned inconvenience, so that likewise a trial shall be taken to find a good well there. The further fortifications where principally still [water is needed]

water about half an hour's distance away has been fetched by digging. The redoubt at Delft on Porto has likewise had the aforementioned inconvenience, so that similarly a trial will be undertaken to find a good well there. The further fortifications that still require attention are principally the small redoubt on the Three Brothers [Nussalant], and Wailapia or Horn, though the latter is not as necessary, as the river there lies at a musket shot's distance from the redoubt. His Excellency Jacob Cops, Resident Extraordinary and Governor in Banda, having arrived here at the Castle on the 25th of November by way of the Uliassers, and having subsequently made a brief expedition on the coast of Hitoe, reported in the assembly at Amboina on the 5th of May 1668 that various redoubts were provided with poor and unsuitable cannon, considering it entirely necessary that this be brought to Your Excellency's attention, with a request to be permitted to enjoy other good cannon in their place. But since this requires somewhat more detailed specification, our intention is to send Captain Paulus Andriesen with the Constable of this Castle by the first opportunity to obtain exact knowledge of that artillery, and furthermore to have examined the military order that is observed everywhere, along with what else depends thereon. Having given attention to the improvement of our powder magazines, we have observed how the south-east corner of this Castle, where one is built with round stones in sand and earth, is floored in such a way that all the rainwater falling into it necessarily also runs against the cellar wall, and for this reason, after good deliberation with the council, it has been determined to floor the aforementioned corner of the building (which stands above the cellar) up to approximately the level of the gun carriage, partly in cement and further in good or sugar lime with the said clinker stone, which has recently been done since the receipt of those materials. The water is taken away on all sides through a suitable gutter, its discharge being outside the Castle, so that we need not doubt that the walls, now having no more influx of moisture, will gradually dry out. It remains yet that the floor of the chamber above the cellar be examined and, if suitable, a pavement of clinker and cement be made over it, or otherwise, as one finds necessary, a new vault be constructed. The other cellar (likewise standing under a chamber) on the north-west corner is around 5 to 6 feet wide all around, was well floored with clinker, whereby it apparently did not have as great a need for moisture as the aforementioned findings. And finally, for several days fire was stoked in them, at which time all the powder was dried with good precaution. Amboina, the 5th of May 1668. We then believed the greatest concern had been overcome, but it did not last long before we received an order to inspect and report that the powder, notwithstanding the aforementioned improvement, lay again as before, due to great dampness of the walls, especially of the first-mentioned cellar. So that now no further remedy remains except the aforementioned alternative, besides still placing a small wall of the same material (although the cellar is narrow enough) against the old one, hoping thereby to achieve the objective, so as not to fall into a lamentable inconvenience. Meanwhile, as much as the opening of the cellars somewhat permits, attention shall be paid to the preservation of the presently good powder. It has been deemed advisable to send the bad and spoiled powder by Meliskerke, in the confidence that the same can be made good in the Batavian mill, the quantity consisting of 200 barrels. The same will, without doubt, go well with the water channels outside, and if it succeeds likewise on the flat roofs, done up to Batavia, it must be good work, not only for the redoubts, but also within this Castle where the buildings stand quite high above and much is always to be done with the roofs. However, it does not appear that we shall be able to make any progress in this this year, since the beams at the north coast of Boero lie felled, and those are to be fetched by the White Lion, principally for the much-needed renewal of the timber yard, for which, due to lack of wood, no progress has yet been able to be made. This matter having been examined and considered with such deliberation that one could hardly think otherwise, or Your Excellency would conform with this proposal, so that the thoughts turn to the strength of the fortifications here, and especially along the Hitoe coast, which by reduction of personnel can only serve to greater hindrance. For this reason, it has been unanimously resolved to hold the building of the aforementioned redoubt in suspense, until further order from Your Excellency or the aforementioned Superintendent. Since then the same has also been understood regarding the projected stone guardhouse on Wey, where the barricade can no longer hold by age, the materials for which are in stock and at hand. --- CHUNK 1 ---
Similarly, understand this regarding the projected stone guardhouse on Weij, where the barricade can no longer be held up by age and nature, the materials for which are in stock and at hand. For the same reasons, the wall around the redoubt Oostburg on Buero is also being kept in abeyance, without, however, allowing the natives any knowledge of these plans, since the same was postponed to the actual and present rainy season, meanwhile this benefits the further works. We have read elsewhere a memorandum from the late Governor Joan van Dam regarding the superfluous redoubts, which is applicable to this matter and time, as well as the advice of the council members against it, which latter principally also bring forward that the same were not only necessary for the resistance against foreign enemies, but especially to keep the Ambonese in proper devotion. But since matters have now taken on a different character, in any case one needs to take knowledge of what the natives are doing and keep them to their duty, no more than one person, whether sergeant or corporal, should be given residence at the command of the two first-mentioned places, in a bamboo house, since no trade or any business is conducted there, which will then save about 25 to 30 men for the first time. Meanwhile, we cannot with the late Governor van Dam deny that if elsewhere new redoubts or fortifications were to be placed in the stead of the old fallen barricades, that the one at Weij, being the only one between Hitoe Lama and the Passo Baguale, should necessarily proceed, just as likewise, regarding the not making of the projected wall at Boero, it may be objected that this outer work, standing under the constraint of the redoubt, brings no difficulty in the garrison, so that in order not to make any errors in this, it has been deemed proper to await further orders, hoping that Your Excellencies will take this postponement in good part.

The ditch around the redoubt Wantrou to Manipa, being 40 feet wide, the ground marshy and raised with a stone wall, having a faucebranne [a type of fortification element] on the inner side, has been completed, or at least so little remains to be done to it that one can say, on Amboina the 5th of May 1668, that this work has been finished. So too the palisade outside the redoubt Middelburg has been made and planted with thorns, but these have died again, because this was done at the end of the past rainy season, which will now be resumed, and better results are to be expected from it, as the report states. The water passage on the beach in front of this Castle, being a work that requires its time, since the same, in order to bring it above water, must be filled up well 4, 5, or 6 feet, but first must be provided with an immovable foundation to the wall of rough and large square-cut stones, for which a good quantity is already at hand and ready to be fetched from the outer places. For the gathering of these, in the past quiet season, namely the month of October, according to the order of the Esteemed Superintendent, the yearly corvée force from Leitimor, Hitoe, Lerique, and Harouca was used. To the wall of rough and large square-cut stones, provision has been made, for which a good quantity is already at hand and ready to be fetched from the outer places. For the gathering of these, in the past quiet season, namely the month of October, according to the order of the Esteemed Superintendent, the yearly corvée force from Leitimor, Hitoe, Lerique, and Harouca was used. Besides this, His Excellency has from the broken Macassar forts sent a quantity of large square stones per Vlieland [ship name] hither, particularly useful for the aforementioned work. However, since with this we cannot make up even a third part of the required circumference, so it shall be our duty, if in the meantime no contrary orders are given, to consider when the suitable time comes whether one should not employ the Leitimor corvée force again in place of the yearly court service for this purpose, seeing that those of the Ulliassers, Buero, Manipa, and Borneo are sufficient for the ordinary inspection. Furthermore, six lime kilns were operated at the same time, both for the service of this water passage and the shipyard, and nothing more has been done here. Now the Hoecker and thereafter, if needed, the Leeuw [ship names] will go to fetch the stone from the places, and we shall then begin with digging and laying of the foundation, which must first be arranged before we can come to the widening of the ditch of this Castle, for one will benefit the other afterwards. Batavia [Batavia, modern Jakarta]. To the Honorable Lord Joan Maatsuiker, Governor General, and the Esteemed Honorable Lords, Council of India, Most Esteemed and Respectable Gentlemen. Most Esteemed Honorable Lords. Your last letter to us, dated the 12th of October, departed on the 13th via the court of Zeeland [Zeeland], and a copy is enclosed herewith. Since then, Raja Palacca has been assisted with the native soldiers and the company of Jancker, while two other Dutch companies were held in reserve. On the following morning, south of the forest of Batta Batta, near the first palisade, there was sharp combat, in which the enemy, encouraged in person by the King and all the great leaders, was continuously reinforced with troops, so that the fighting became fierce and came to close quarters. By God's grace, our men carried off the advantage, having obtained over 100 heads, and according to the reports subsequently received, they also carried away well over 100 more, not counting the wounded. We lost 15 men on the 15th, and among them 4 brave fellows, besides 33 wounded, and one of the native soldiers was shot in the arm. We have since understood that if we had pressed further forward, the enemy would have been completely routed and would likely have abandoned the new palisade entirely. However, it was high noon, very hot, the troops were weary, and they also seemed satisfied with the advantage gained. It became clear to us that for the most part their courage had already sunk considerably beneath their belts. The following morning, the enemy appeared again under various banners at the same place, but we did not allow anyone to go out against them, in order to pursue other work (which was more necessary at that time), so they went away again in the heat of the midday sun. On the 17th, at night, our men were

--- CHUNK 2 ---
again out on a raiding expedition, but they were discovered far too early. Having made the last plunder on the 10th, the enemy had posted sharp and strong guards everywhere, so that now, having accomplished nothing, with some houses burned to coals, they returned. In view of the fact that all the women and children from hereabouts had been brought to other villages for better security, and since now for the first time with this plundering there was no more to be gained, by day some small parties went out against each other, in which now from one side and then from the other, a head or two or three was won and lost. So the thoughts turned again to the lower palisade, near Raja Palacca, which from the outside seemed somewhat damaged by the shooting of two or three coconut trees, so that another 8-pound cannon was dragged there. With this, having shot rather heavily, Raja was assisted with the native soldiers and 8 or 10 sailors with hand grenades and fire pots. Between the 22nd and 23rd of October, at night, they went at it for the third time, meeting with reasonable resistance, but with the throwing of that fire weapon it was soon overcome. From the spilled blood, one could discern that damage must have been inflicted on the enemy, which was subsequently estimated by us at 30 dead. The garrison was between 300 and 400 men strong and had been commanded by Galeran Manassa, a Makassar man, in great trust by his king. A woman and a boy were found there. Furthermore: 1 standard, 2 flags, 1 fine metal cannon, 2 small metal swivel guns, 10 pounds of gunpowder, 20 muskets and musket pouches, and 20 cannon balls, besides some sharp weapons that they had gathered here and there from our cannon fire. Two bougies [uncertain: possibly a type of soldier or officer] died in this action. 7 wounded from musket fire, and 1 from a kris [a type of dagger], but without serious danger. A wound received by one of our sailors from musket fire caused no harm through timely use of antidote. At this palisade, with a row of heavily filled sandbags, firmly tied at a distance of about 100 paces, there was another stronger nest, though not much larger. Between the 23rd and 24th, at night, it was attacked in the usual manner, but it took a good 2 hours before one could get under it and use the grenades. Even then the enemy did not come out well until they saw them climbing up. 5 dead were found there, with 2 metal cannon pieces, 1 large metal falconet with a chamber for it, 1 flag, 30 muskets with their pouches, 6 muskets, and furthermore some clothing and other rags that the garrison, fleeing, had not been able to take with them. Raja was struck by a musket ball, and about 20 with him, but they were not particularly inconvenienced by it. These good successes, as we were assured, caused the King of Makassar great distress, and gave a considerable refreshment to our men.
